column4: The section explicitly sets أَلَمْ يَأْنِ beside late remembrance: here believers are asked whether the time has come for hearts to soften to God's remembrance while response is still possible.
The same question أَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ is asked after a clear messenger has already come; it makes remembrance futile because its earlier occasion was rejected.
The Hour's sudden arrival is followed by فَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمْ ... ذِكْرَىٰهُمْ, exactly the section's image of recollection arriving only when its usable time has closed.
After judgment they profess belief, but وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ ٱلتَّنَاوُشُ describes trying to reach it from a far place; this supplies the spatial reach behind the section's backward-stretching hand.
At the great catastrophe, the human being remembers مَا سَعَىٰ, directly matching the section's person who remembers past striving when Hell is brought into view.
This ayah brings ٱلطَّآمَّةُ ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ; it opens the judgment scene whose next ayah supplies the belated remembrance.
Hell is exposed لِمَن يَرَىٰ immediately after the person's remembrance, completing the same sight-and-recollection sequence as 89:23.
The command that every soul inspect مَّا قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍ turns the regret of 89:24 into a present practice: send something ahead while tomorrow is still ahead.
On the near Day, a person sees مَا قَدَّمَتْ يَدَاهُ and the unbeliever wishes to be dust; sight of what the hands sent ahead produces the same too-late wish.
The human being is informed on that Day of مَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ, expanding the section's one wished-for advance into a complete reckoning of what was sent ahead and left behind.
عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ مَّا قَدَّمَتْ وَأَخَّرَ joins the section's two key terms, soul and sending ahead, at the moment when the world's order breaks open.
The declaration that the Hereafter is لَهِىَ ٱلْحَيَوَانُ identifies it as the real life, explaining why the regretful speaker can finally call that destination “my life.”
At the arrival of death the person pleads رَبِّ ٱرْجِعُونِ; the requested return is the last attempt to recover the time that the section says has passed.
He asks to return and do righteousness in what he left, but كَلَّا closes the request and the barrier remains until resurrection; no deed can now be sent ahead.
God takes the souls at death and those not dead during sleep, retaining one and sending the other back to an appointed term; it stages the section's breath-like departure and permitted return.
The life-breath reaches ٱلتَّرَاقِىَ, locating the soul's departure at the collarbones just before the final driving described later in the passage.
The bystanders ask who can provide a cure or incantation, giving the human side of the deathbed scene after the soul reaches the collarbones.
The dying person realizes أَنَّهُ ٱلْفِرَاقُ, naming the separation that the section imagines through breath leaving the body.
One leg is wound around the other, adding the body's final helplessness before the soul's movement toward its Lord.
Believing hearts become tranquil بِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ; this joins timely remembrance to the settled state embodied by ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ.
The dawn is sworn by إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ, “when it breathes”; this is the Qur'anic breathing image that makes visible the dictionary source's outward movement of نَفَس.
God fashions the human and breathes into him of His spirit before granting hearing, sight, and hearts; breath here marks the body's becoming a living, perceiving person.
The command فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ asks for reminder while it can benefit, the live side of 89:23's question about a reminder that can no longer do so.
The one who fears receives the reminder, identifying the responsive hearer before the passage turns to the person who avoids it.
The most wretched person avoids the reminder, supplying the earlier refusal that makes later recognition in the Fire useless.
That person enters the great Fire; it gives the destination reached after refusing the reminder in the preceding ayah.
In that Fire the person neither dies nor lives, a stark boundary around “life” that clarifies why the Hereafter can be encountered without becoming the wished-for life.
Success belongs to one who purifies the self, showing a path from the commanding or reproaching self toward the settled soul.
The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and prays; remembrance here becomes action sent ahead rather than a thought recovered too late.
Preferring ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا identifies the mistaken placement of “my life” that 89:24 corrects only after judgment.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, stating why deeds must be prepared for that life rather than for the preferred nearer one.
The transgressor preferred worldly life, giving the choice that precedes the exposed Hell and belated recollection in this same passage.
Hell is the refuge of the one who preferred worldly life, connecting that preference to the scene in which Hell becomes visible.
The one who fears standing before the Lord restrains ٱلنَّفْسَ from desire; the self is disciplined before judgment instead of regretting after it.
The Garden is that person's refuge, completing the alternative to both exposed Hell and the wish that nothing had been sent ahead.
The recipient of the right-hand book says he knew he would meet his account; remembered accountability shaped action before the meeting rather than arising after it.
He is then فِى عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ, a pleasing life that answers both “my life” and the satisfied soul's state.
The Garden's people are told to eat and drink for بِمَآ أَسْلَفْتُمْ فِى ٱلْأَيَّامِ ٱلْخَالِيَةِ; prior deeds have actually reached the life for which 89:24 wishes it had prepared.
The person given the book in the left hand cries يَٰلَيْتَنِى لَمْ أُوتَ كِتَٰبِيَهْ, another judgment-day wish produced by a record that can no longer be changed.
He wishes he had never known his account, specifying the knowledge whose arrival now only deepens the preceding regret.
He wishes the former death had been final, the inverse of recognizing the Hereafter as the true life.
His wealth has not availed him, exposing the worldly possession that failed to become something sent ahead.
His authority has vanished, completing the stripping away of the worldly measures by which he had understood his life.
Heavy scales identify the person whose earlier deeds have weight at judgment, the fulfilled counterpart to wishing one had prepared.
That person is فِى عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ, another direct joining of true life with satisfaction.
Faces are joyful on that Day, beginning the opposite outcome to the face and voice of belated regret.
Those faces are لِّسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ, satisfied with their prior striving; 79:35's remembered striving has here become a source of contentment.
They are in a high Garden, giving the destination of the satisfied striving named immediately before it.
Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as it deserves while believing has a striving that is appreciated; this is deliberate preparation for that life.
Eternal Gardens culminate in رَّضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ, the mutual satisfaction unfolded in the address to the satisfied, approved soul.
Angels descend on those steadfast in saying “Our Lord is God” and tell them not to fear or grieve; it closely parallels the calm divine reception of the settled soul.
The angels declare themselves allies in this life and the Hereafter and promise whatever the souls desire, extending that peaceful reception across both lives.
The promised welcome is hospitality from the Forgiving, Merciful, completing the hospitable address that precedes entry into the Garden.
The Garden is brought near to the mindful, placing the promised destination before the returning person without the exposure of Hell.
It is promised to every أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ, one repeatedly returning and keeping faith, giving a lived form of “return to your Lord.”
The entrant feared the Merciful unseen and came with قَلْبٍ مُّنِيبٍ, a heart already turned back before the meeting.
ٱدْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ addresses them with peaceful entry and calls it the day of abiding, closely matching the settled soul's invitation into the Garden.
God's servants are addressed on that Day with no fear and no grief, the same reassuring stance as the call to the tranquil soul.
The addressees are those who believed in the signs and submitted, identifying the prior response that made the peaceful address possible.
“Enter the Garden” is spoken to them in joy, directly paralleling the command that concludes the settled soul's return.
Angels take the good while saying “Peace upon you; enter the Garden for what you did,” combining a gentle taking of souls with peaceful entry earned by prior action.
The righteous enter perpetual Gardens with their righteous kin, giving the communal Garden entry promised after the individual soul's return.
Angels enter through every gate saying “Peace upon you for your patience,” making prior endurance the reason for the peaceful reception.
Every soul finds its good and evil deeds present and wishes a vast distance from the evil; what was done has arrived before it, and wishing cannot remove it.
The person reminded of God's signs turns away and forgets مَا قَدَّمَتْ يَدَاهُ; it joins refused remembrance to the deeds later recovered too late.
God records مَا قَدَّمُوا۟ وَءَاثَٰرَهُمْ, preserving both what people send ahead and the traces left behind for the resurrection account.
Whatever good people send ahead لِأَنفُسِكُم is found with God, making the section's “for my life” a present command with a promised destination.
Whatever good believers send ahead for themselves will be found with God as something better and greater in reward; the provision survives its senders.
This ayah joins two section words: أَنَّىٰ in the sense “however” and the command وَقَدِّمُوا۟ لِأَنفُسِكُمْ, turning future provision into an instruction addressed to embodied life.
The text condemns what their souls قَدَّمَتْ لَهُمْ: divine anger and lasting punishment; a soul can send ruin ahead as concretely as it can send good.
Punishment is said to be بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ, so what the hands advanced becomes the ground of the later encounter rather than disappearing into the past.
The same formula, بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ, is spoken in the death scene where angels strike the unbelievers, joining prior deeds to their immediate recompense.
The sufferer is told the burning punishment is for what his hands sent ahead, repeating the exact moral motion behind 89:24's regret.
A messenger is sent lest people blame a calamity on مَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ and ask why no warner came; warning preserves a time for response before regret.
When the cosmic veils are removed, every soul knows مَّآ أَحْضَرَتْ, what it has brought with it; deeds are present at the destination reached by the soul.
Every soul is pledged for what it earned, binding the soul's final condition to the action it sent through its worldly life.
Each person's deed-record is fastened to his neck and brought out as an opened book at resurrection; the past accompanies the person bodily into judgment.
“Read your book; your own soul is sufficient as reckoner today” makes self-knowledge unavoidable once the time for changing the record is gone.
People issue forth separately to be shown their deeds, beginning a judgment scene in which nothing sent ahead remains hidden.
Whoever did an atom's weight of good sees it, making the smallest prior provision present in the later life.
Whoever did an atom's weight of evil sees it, completing the exactness of that recovered past.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it treats the soul as something formed for a moral history, not merely an escaping breath.
The soul is inspired with its wickedness and mindfulness, naming the opposing possibilities behind the commanding, reproaching, and settled states.
Success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, describing the transformation whose settled result can return contentedly.
Failure belongs to the one who buries or corrupts the soul, the opposing formation that ends in belated recognition.
Whoever purifies himself does so for his own soul, and the destination is God; self-purification is preparation carried all the way to the return.
When believers wrong themselves they remember God, seek forgiveness, and do not knowingly persist; remembrance still repairs action here because it comes before judgment.
A soul cries “Alas for what I neglected concerning God” lest it face punishment; the warning voices the regret now so it need not be spoken too late.
The same soul imagines saying that, had God guided it, it would have been mindful; this exposes the excuse that follows neglected warning.
On seeing punishment it asks for another turn so it can be among the doers of good, exactly the impossible effort to send something ahead after arrival.
The answer recalls that signs did come but were denied in arrogance; the lost opportunity, not lack of a reminder, caused the late plea.
Standing over the Fire, they wish to be returned so they could stop denying the signs and become believers; visible punishment triggers an unusable resolve.
What they concealed has appeared, yet a return would lead them back to the same prohibition; it denies that a spoken late wish proves a changed soul.
The guilty lower their heads before their Lord and ask to be returned to do righteousness now that they see and hear with certainty.
When the promised outcome arrives, rejecters admit the messengers told the truth and ask for intercession or a return to act differently; their selves are already lost.
People are told to spend before death comes, when a soul will ask for a short delay to give charity and become righteous; present giving is something that can still be sent ahead.
God will not delay any soul once its term arrives, closing the very interval requested in the preceding plea.
People cry from Hell to be taken out so they can do other than before, but are reminded that they had a sufficient lifespan and a warner.
The people of the Blaze say that if they had listened or reasoned they would not be its companions; understanding arrives only inside the consequence.
They confess their sin, confirming that the preceding wish is acknowledgment after the usable time for hearing has passed.
When they see God's punishment they finally profess faith in God alone and reject former partners, a belief produced by unveiled consequence.
Their faith does not benefit them once they have seen the punishment; this directly states the rule implicit in “how can remembrance benefit him?”
Repentance is not for the person who persists until death arrives and then says “I repent now”; the ayah marks the temporal boundary of useful recollection.
At drowning Pharaoh declares belief in Israel's God, offering a historical scene of certainty and confession arriving with destruction.
“Now?” answers that confession by recalling his earlier rebellion and corruption, denying the saving force of recognition at the closed moment.
The stupor of death brings the truth the person had been avoiding; the previously evaded reality becomes immediate when action is ending.
The soul or life-breath reaches the throat, opening a deathbed scene closely parallel to its reaching the collarbones.
Those present look on as it reaches the throat, stressing their inability to stop or reverse the departure.
God is nearer to the dying person than the witnesses although they do not see, placing the hidden taking beside the visible body.
The listeners are challenged, if they are truly beyond recompense, setting up return of the departing life as the test of that claim.
“Bring it back” makes the breath-like return that humans cannot command explicit; only God sends a soul back from sleep or holds it at death.
God takes people by night, knows what they acquired by day, and raises them again until the fixed term; each waking is a temporary return before the final one.
The angel of death takes people fully and then they are returned to their Lord, joining the soul's taking to its ultimate direction.
Every soul tastes death, receives full reward at resurrection, and learns that worldly life was deceptive enjoyment; soul, death, reckoning, and the lesser life meet in one ayah.
Every soul tastes death, is tested with bad and good, and is returned to God; embodied life is an examination whose return discloses its result.
Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, placing the soul's destination beyond the death that ends its present action.
God created death and life to test who is best in deed; life is the interval for producing the action later remembered and judged.
People were lifeless, God gave them life, will cause them to die and give them life again, then they return to Him; the full movement belongs to God.
After two deaths and two lives, the condemned confess their sins and ask whether there is any way out; renewed life produces recognition but no new earthly term.
Turning away from God's remembrance yields a constricted life and blind resurrection, directly tying refused remembrance to a damaged worldly life and later exposure.
The resurrected person asks why he has been raised blind although he once saw, voicing the shocked self-reading of judgment.
God answers that signs came and were forgotten, so the person is forgotten that Day; the judgment condition corresponds to the earlier treatment of remembrance.
The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger, a bodily image of regret for the route not taken while time was open.
He wishes he had not taken a particular person as intimate friend, locating the worldly relation that shaped his lost path.
The friend led him away from the reminder after it had come, connecting the judgment wish to an earlier, received remembrance that was abandoned.
With faces turned in the Fire, they wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; the lost action becomes clear only inside punishment.
They explain that obedience to leaders and great ones led them from the way, identifying the prior allegiance behind their regret.
They ask for doubled punishment and a great curse on those leaders, showing how late memory assigns blame without reopening action.
Humanity is addressed as laboring toward its Lord and destined to meet Him; every present exertion is already traveling to the encounter.
The person given the record in the right hand begins the favorable version of that meeting.
He receives an easy accounting, the outcome of deeds prepared before the meeting rather than a late wish.
He returns joyfully to his people, a peaceful return that echoes the settled soul's contented return.
The one given the record behind his back begins the opposite return scene.
He calls for destruction, another judgment-day utterance whose wish cannot change the record.
He enters a Blaze, giving the consequence that prompts the preceding cry.
He had been joyful among his people, showing a worldly contentment whose object and duration differed from the joyful return in 84:9.
He thought he would never return, exposing the false belief beneath his former ease.
His Lord was always seeing him, correcting the denied return with the continuous divine knowledge that grounds his account.

At death the angels stretch out their hands and command wrongdoers أَخْرِجُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمُ, followed by humiliating punishment; forced extraction is the sharp opposite of the tranquil soul being invited to return.
إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ ٱلْمَسَاقُ says the final driving is to the Lord; the section explicitly sets this compelled movement against the settled soul's addressed return.
The soul that relentlessly commands evil is an opposing state to the soul whose turmoil has settled and which can return well pleased.
Unbelievers are driven in groups to Hell and questioned by its keepers about the warners; compulsion and accusation reverse the tranquil soul's welcome.
The mindful are conducted in groups to the Garden and greeted with peace by its keepers; this parallels the destination while distinguishing a communal escort from the section's intimate call.
Those who are content with and reassured by worldly life while heedless of the signs attach tranquility to the wrong life, reversing the settled soul's readiness for return.
أَنَّىٰ يُحْىِۦ هَٰذِهِ ٱللَّهُ asks how God will revive a ruined town after death, and God demonstrates revival; “how?” opens onto divine life-giving here but closes onto human benefit in 89:23.
Angels take those who wronged their souls; their late submission and denial of wrongdoing receive rebuttal, unlike the good soul's truthful, peaceful reception.
Angels take the unbelievers while striking faces and backs and ordering them to taste burning; this violent taking opposes the call to the settled soul.
The angels strike faces and backs when taking those who followed what angered God, another forced departure set against a willing return.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness at judgment; the driven arrival forms a boundary around the exceptional gentleness of “return to your Lord.”
Those killed in God's way must not be called dead but living, though people do not perceive it; apparent bodily death does not exhaust the Qur'anic field of life.
Those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord and provided for, locating life and provision beyond the worldly ending.
The criminal in Hell neither dies nor lives, a negative limit-case that separates mere continued existence from the “life” for which one should prepare.
Hell's people are neither finished by death nor relieved of punishment, showing an afterlife continuation that is not the desired life.
Death comes to the punished person from every direction, yet he does not die; this grotesque suspension clarifies the section's richer use of “my life.”
The Garden's people taste no death beyond the first death and are protected from Hell, the positive boundary opposite the state that is neither dead nor alive.
After being told to enter the Garden, the slain believer wishes his people knew of his forgiveness; this post-death wish seeks their benefit rather than repairing his own missed action.
What he wishes them to know is that his Lord forgave and honored him, completing the generous reversal of the condemned person's self-directed “if only.”
The ruined garden owner wrings his hands and wishes he had not associated anyone with his Lord; this worldly loss still dramatizes regret before the final judgment scene.
Mary asks أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى وَلَدٌ, “how can I have a child?”, and the answer asserts God's creative command; an apparently closed “how” here opens into new life by divine power.
Mary again asks أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى غُلَٰمٌ with no man having touched her; the question concerns the seemingly impossible arrival of life, unlike the impossible recovery of spent moral time.
The oath by the self-reproaching soul names an inner state in which wrongdoing is recognized; it can be read as a stage between the commanding self and settled tranquility.
Once the human is fashioned and God breathes into him of His spirit, the angels are commanded to prostrate; breathed spirit marks the completion of embodied human life.
The repeated creation formula joins shaping with breathing of spirit, reinforcing breath as the threshold of living personhood.
God breathes of His spirit into the woman who guarded her chastity and makes her and her son a sign; breath imagery accompanies extraordinary human life.
Mary's story again uses breathed spirit and then describes her faithfulness, linking life-giving breath with a soul formed by belief and obedience.
Abraham asks to see how God revives the dead so that his heart may be reassured; tranquility here grows through witnessed resurrection rather than through denial of it.
God makes promised help good news so that hearts may be reassured by it; the settled condition is rooted in trust that comes before the final meeting.
The parallel promise of angelic help is made so hearts may be reassured, another concrete use of the state named by ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ.
The disciples say the heavenly table would reassure their hearts and let them know the truth, showing reassurance sought through a confirming sign.
A heart can remain مُطْمَئِنٌّۢ بِٱلْإِيمَٰنِ even under coercion, locating tranquility in durable faith rather than outward ease.
On the Day truthfulness benefits the truthful, eternal Gardens culminate in God being pleased with them and they with Him; mutual approval supplies the horizon of the pleased soul.
The foremost believers receive God's pleasure, their pleasure in Him, and eternal Gardens; the satisfied state is joined to a life of prior faithful action.
Those supported with spirit and admitted to eternal Gardens are described by رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ, another communal form of the soul's mutual contentment.
The most mindful gives wealth to purify himself, making purification an outward deed sent toward the lasting outcome.
His giving seeks only the face of his Lord Most High, fixing the true destination of what he sends ahead.
وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ promises that he will be satisfied, a future contentment produced by God-directed preparation.
Garden dwellers are told that their reward is theirs and their striving has been appreciated; the later address confirms that their earlier effort arrived.
The right-hand recipient openly invites others to read his book; unlike the regretful speaker, he can face the record that reached him.
The pleasing life is located in a high Garden, identifying the lasting home for which the favorable record prepared.
Its fruits are brought near, turning the abstract future provision into a provision now within reach.
They will never wish for death because of what their hands sent ahead; prior deeds shape even what a person dares to wish at the threshold of return.
The same refusal to wish for death is grounded in what their hands have sent ahead, repeating the link between advance action and fear of the meeting.
When disaster strikes because of what their hands sent ahead, they come swearing good intentions; consequence produces a belated reinterpretation of their acts.
The record is laid open, the guilty fear its contents, and all they did is found present; nothing from the lived past is too small to arrive.
A Day of return to God is feared, when every soul is paid fully for what it earned; return and individual recompense meet directly.
Every soul comes pleading for itself and is paid fully for what it did, showing the soul speaking only after its deeds have become fixed evidence.
A soul can be held for what it earned, and no ransom or intercession can release it; acquisition in this life determines its later captivity.
Destroyed generations cried out, but it was no time for escape; the brief formula captures a call made only after the door of response had closed.
When the true promise draws near, unbelievers stare and admit they were heedless and unjust; unveiled reality forces the remembrance that heedlessness postponed.
The veil of heedlessness is removed and sight becomes sharp that Day; late clarity explains how the person can suddenly remember the life just completed.
Those facing punishment ask for a brief respite so they can answer the call and follow the messengers; even a little returned time is now unavailable.
When wrongdoers see punishment they ask whether there is any way of return, another attempt to reverse direction only at the destination.
The condemned wish for another turn so they could become believers; the wish names a new identity but cannot supply a new span of action.
Followers wish for a return so they could disown their leaders as the leaders disowned them; God shows their deeds as regrets from which they cannot leave the Fire.
Whoever blinds himself to the Merciful's remembrance is assigned a devil as companion, tracing a present refusal of remembrance into a lasting relation.
On arriving before God, that person wishes the companion were as far away as the two easts; the desired distance appears only after companionship has done its work.
Competitive accumulation distracts people, naming the worldly absorption that keeps them from preparing for their real life.
The distraction continues until they visit the graves, setting death as the point at which its hold is finally exposed.
“You will soon know” warns of knowledge arriving after the distraction, akin to recollection at the revealed consequence.
The warning “again, you will soon know” intensifies the staged arrival of certainty beyond the grave.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the Hereafter is better for the mindful; it distinguishes the life lived as distraction from the life worth preparing for.
Worldly life is likened to admired vegetation that dries and crumbles, followed by punishment or forgiveness in the Hereafter; passing growth cannot be the lasting “my life.”
The believer calls worldly life only temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the enduring abode, a direct correction of where lasting life is located.
People love ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ, the immediate life, naming the temporal preference that leaves no provision for later.
They leave the Hereafter, completing the opposition between immediate attachment and the destination toward which the death scene soon drives them.
People love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy Day, treating the coming reality as if it could remain behind them.
Those who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter also obstruct God's way, so the misplaced preference becomes a course of action rather than a mere opinion.
Disbelief after faith is explained by preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, showing how the chosen “life” forms the soul before return.
Believers are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter, whose scale makes worldly enjoyment little.
Worldly enjoyment is little and the Hereafter better for the mindful; the comparison directs present restraint toward the longer life.
People rejoice in worldly life even though it is only a small enjoyment compared with the Hereafter, exposing joy attached to what passes.
What people receive is worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for trusting believers; enduring provision lies at the destination.
Worldly goods are enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting; it asks the hearer to reason before the comparison becomes visible.
Worldly life is rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry debris scattered by winds, a scene of growth and breath-like dispersal that measures its passing span.
Wealth and children adorn worldly life, but enduring good deeds are better with the Lord for reward and hope; deeds are the portion that can be sent beyond it.
Worldly life is play and diversion, while faith and mindfulness yield rewards without consuming people's wealth; action can be converted into lasting provision.
People know only the outward aspect of worldly life and are heedless of the Hereafter; knowledge of the surface coexists with forgetfulness of the true destination.
Guests are told not to wait for a meal's إِنَىٰهُ, its proper readiness time; the cognate gives the source section's time-root a concrete sense of a moment becoming due.
Zechariah asks Mary أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا about the source of her provision, illustrating the source section's “from where?” sense of the same word.
Believers are promised قَدَمَ صِدْقٍ with their Lord, a true prior standing that closely matches the dictionary source's “preceding قدم” and enduring good already with God.
A span of time passed over the human when he was not a thing مَّذْكُورًا; the remembrance root here means being mentioned and frames human life within time before conscious memory.
Humanity is created from a mixed drop as a test and given hearing and sight, specifying the embodied, responsible life that follows the unmentioned state.
The rejecters do not believe until they see the painful punishment, making sight of the consequence the point at which their former refusal finally breaks.
The punishment comes suddenly while they are unaware, closing the interval in which remembrance could still have become action.
Only then do they ask whether they will be granted respite, another request for usable time made after that time has ended.
The unbelievers will come to wish that they had been Muslims; the future wish states the same late recognition without yet staging all its consequences.
Eating, enjoyment, and distracting hopes occupy them until they come to know, identifying the nearer life that postpones the recognition predicted just before.
A Garden speaker asks whether they are then never to die, confronting the permanence of the life reached after the first death.
The speaker specifies that only the first death has occurred and that no punishment follows, marking the Garden's life as secure beyond death.
“This is the great triumph” names that death-surviving outcome as the true success.
“For the like of this let the workers work” turns the unveiled afterlife into a present directive to send effort toward it.
God has apportioned death among people and cannot be forestalled, placing the end of the acting life under divine measure.
God can replace people with their likes and bring them forth in a form they do not know, so departure does not limit His power to originate another life.
People already know the first creation and are asked why they do not remember; remembered origin is offered before death as evidence for renewed life.
The deathbed passage now distinguishes the departing person who is among those brought near, beginning the peaceful outcome of the soul just taken.
That person receives rest, fragrant provision, and a Garden of delight, closely paralleling the tranquil soul's welcoming destination.
A second favorable case identifies the departing person as one of the companions of the right.
The greeting “peace to you” follows for the companion of the right, giving a gentle reception after the soul's irretrievable departure.
The departing denier who went astray begins the opposing outcome, showing why not every soul leaves in tranquility.
Boiling water is that denier's first hospitality, reversing the fragrant provision of the one brought near.
Burning in Hell completes the opposed reception immediately after the throat-and-return challenge.
The human forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones; forgetfulness of origin produces denial of the later life.
The answer says the One who originated the bones the first time will revive them, replacing forgotten origin with a timely reminder of return.
God ends the quarrel at judgment by saying that He had sent the warning ahead to them; advance warning, unlike their late dispute, arrived while response remained possible.
A human being has only what he strove for, making prior striving the actual provision later remembered or enjoyed.
That striving will be seen, so effort from the hidden past becomes visible at the destination.
It is then repaid with the fullest recompense, completing the movement from striving through sight to result.
The coming Hour is kept hidden so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for; the concealed deadline makes present striving meaningful.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, stating the passing-versus-lasting measure behind sending provision ahead.
Everything perishes except God's face, judgment belongs to Him, and people return to Him; passing things, enduring sovereignty, and return meet in one boundary.
Everyone upon the earth passes away, stripping worldly life of any claim to permanence.
The majestic, generous face of the Lord remains, supplying the enduring counterpart toward which the departing soul returns.
Pilgrims are commanded to take provision, then told that the best provision is mindfulness; the journey's literal supplies become a concrete model for moral provision sent toward arrival.
Believers are commanded to answer God and the Messenger when called to what gives them life, placing life in a responsive act that must occur before the final gathering.
A believing doer of righteousness is promised a good life and later reward according to the best deeds, joining lived action to both present and future life.
The deniers say there is only worldly life and no resurrection, stating exactly the mistaken location of life that the later judgment scene overturns.
When made to stand before their Lord they admit the resurrection is true and are told to taste punishment for denial; certainty arrives at the closed moment.
Those deceived by worldly life forgot the meeting of their Day, so they are forgotten then; their treatment of remembrance becomes their judgment condition.
They are told that they are forgotten that Day just as they forgot its meeting, making the final exclusion answer their earlier cultivated forgetfulness.
They are told to taste the result of forgetting the meeting of their Day and that they have been forgotten; the missed remembrance becomes irreversible encounter.
The question whether humans thought they were created aimlessly and would not return exposes the false premise behind living without preparation.
The greatest terror does not grieve the righteous, and angels receive them with “this is your promised Day”; peaceful angelic reception closely parallels the address to the tranquil soul.
Those who say “Our Lord is God” and remain upright have no fear or grief, describing the stable formation that precedes a calm return.
They remain in the Garden as recompense for what they did, connecting that settled state to deeds already completed.
“Enter it in peace, secure” is a direct Garden welcome that parallels the tranquil soul's commanded entry.
At the arrival of death God's messengers take the person without neglect, identifying the agents and exactness of the soul's departure.
They are then returned to God, their true Master, whose judgment is decisive; the taking in the preceding ayah has a stated destination.
Those who answer calamity with “we belong to God and to Him we return” voice the return while still living, rather than learning its direction only when driven.
God makes sleep a repose and the day a rising, giving each daily return of consciousness the resurrection pattern that 39:42 locates in taken and released souls.
At the trumpet blast people emerge from graves and hasten to their Lord, staging bodily return after the soul's earlier departure.
They cry out about who raised them from their sleeping place, then acknowledge the Merciful's promise and the messengers' truth; awakening brings belated recognition.
The death people flee will meet them; afterward they return to the Knower and are informed of what they did, joining unavoidable departure, return, and recovered action.
When certain signs of the Lord arrive, new belief or belief that had earned no good no longer benefits a soul; the ayah explicitly marks the boundary of useful faith.
People who have transgressed against themselves are told not to despair of divine mercy, opening a present path for the soul before the later regret speech.
They are commanded to return to their Lord and submit before punishment comes, the actionable return that prevents an impossible request to return afterward.
They are told to follow the best revelation before punishment comes suddenly and unnoticed, identifying what must be done before the soul says “alas.”
Those who forgot God were made to forget their own souls; failed remembrance deforms the very self that must later return.
When a satanic impulse touches the mindful, they remember and immediately see clearly; this is timely recollection that changes the present state.
Revelation makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance, giving remembrance an embodied movement toward settled receptivity.
God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, then asks أَنَّىٰ people are turned away; the section's “how?” word is joined directly to life's boundary.
God originates creation and repeats it, followed by فَأَنَّىٰ تُؤْفَكُونَ; the same question-word challenges refusal of renewed life.
A lifeless earth trembles and grows when watered, and its reviver will revive the dead; growing life becomes a visible analogy for afterlife.
The effects of mercy show earth revived after death, and the same God will revive the dead; the growing sense of life points beyond bodily death.
On the Day when wealth and children do not benefit, ordinary measures of a successful life cannot serve as provision.
Only one who comes to God with a sound heart benefits, offering a close inner parallel to the soul that arrives settled and fit for welcome.
Whoever hopes to meet the Lord is told to do righteous work and avoid associating anyone in worship; expected meeting becomes present preparation.
People come to God individually as first created and leave granted possessions behind; what was treated as “my life” cannot accompany the returning soul.
People are warned of a Day when parent and child cannot avail each other and told not to be deceived by worldly life; the true promise demands preparation before kinship and possessions fall away.
On that Day no soul controls anything for another soul and command belongs to God, isolating each returning soul with its fixed record.
Pharaoh goes ahead of his people on resurrection day and leads them into the Fire; this ruinous human “advance” reverses sending good ahead to God.
The deniers say there is only worldly life, that people die and live, and that time destroys them; their compressed account excludes the true afterlife later encountered.
The chiefs claim there is only worldly life, generations dying and living with no resurrection; the denial gives the direct opposite of “my life” correctly placed beyond death.

A town was secure and tranquil with abundant provision, then ingratitude turned its state into hunger and fear; outward ease is shown to be a reversible tranquility unlike the faithful soul's settledness.
A person serving God on an edge feels reassured when good arrives but turns away under trial, losing both lives; conditional ease is the opposite of a soul stabilized through the test.
Unbelievers carry the zeal of ignorance while God sends tranquility upon His Messenger and believers, showing divine settledness overcoming an agitated moral state.
Angels take those who wronged their souls and question their excuse before Hell becomes their refuge; this interrogated taking reverses the tranquil soul's unforced welcome.
No community can advance or delay its fixed term, supplying the temporal limit beneath the unbelievers' later wish in 15:2.
The revelation is itself a reminder, presenting remembrance in an available form before it becomes a recovered past.
Whoever wills may remember it, describing the open agency that contrasts with remembrance after judgment has arrived.
The warning is called a reminder, locating its purpose before the hearer reaches the threatened scene.
Whoever wills may remember it, another formulation of accessible recollection during the acting life.
When harm strikes because of what people's hands sent ahead, they despair; the same advance-action idiom operates inside worldly consequence.
A calamity caused by what human hands sent ahead exposes human ingratitude, showing prior action arriving as present condition.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, binding the soul's final condition to its completed action.
Creation in truth culminates in every soul being repaid for what it earned, making embodied life accountable rather than aimless.
When people are gathered for the certain Day, every soul is paid fully for what it earned, specifying the individual settlement of the record.
That Day every soul is repaid for what it earned and no injustice occurs, emphasizing immediacy once the judgment moment arrives.
God repays every soul for what it earned, the final destination of action performed in the preceding life.
Just scales are set for resurrection and even a mustard seed is brought forward, so no soul loses the smallest provision it made.
Enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and return, repeating the distinction between what passes and what reaches its destination.
The human is asked whether he thinks he will be left without purpose, challenging life understood without test or return.
The Creator of the human stages is surely able to revive the dead, answering the aimlessness challenged earlier in the passage.
God sends tranquility into believers' hearts so their faith increases, an indirect account of how a soul becomes settled through divine action.
God knows what is in the believers' hearts, is pleased with them, sends tranquility upon them, and rewards them, joining inner settlement with divine approval.
When the messengers take the wrongdoers' souls, they ask where the invoked partners are, and the dying admit those partners have vanished.
The return is to the Lord, a compact statement of the direction spoken more gently to the tranquil soul.
When wrongdoers see the punishment it is neither lightened nor delayed, so recognition at sight creates no new interval for action.
Satan makes his party forget God's remembrance, tracing final loss back to an active worldly production of forgetfulness.
Zechariah asks أَنَّىٰ he can have a son in old age with a barren wife; “how?” frames life that appears humanly unavailable but remains possible to God.
Zechariah's repeated “how can I have a son?” again places the section's question-word at the boundary between barrenness, age, and divinely given life.
Human development from a drop through womb and maturity, alongside dead earth revived by rain, is presented as evidence for resurrection; growing, embodied, and restored life meet in one proof.
No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow or in what land it will die, preserving the hidden deadline that makes advance preparation necessary.
The trumpet causes all in heavens and earth to fall dead except whom God wills, then a second blast raises them looking on; death and returned awareness are separated only by divine command.
Whoever brings a good deed receives better than it and is safe from that Day's terror, a prepared deed issuing in inward security.
God saves the mindful in their place of success so evil does not touch them and they do not grieve, an indirect parallel to the tranquil soul's fearless reception.
Garden dwellers are told that they inherited the Garden for what they used to do, making entry the arrived result of prior action.
The Garden entrants praise God for fulfilling the promise and letting them settle wherever they wish, voicing contentment after the peaceful welcome of 39:73.
The Garden is said to be inherited for what its people used to do, repeating the direct passage from earlier work to lasting abode.
The Lord promises to give until the addressee is satisfied, a prophetic instance of future contentment grounded in divine giving.
The companions of the right are excepted from the rule that every soul is pledged for its earning, marking the favorable class within that soul-and-deed formula.
Each person remains pledged for what he earned even when believing descendants are joined to their family, preserving individual moral possession within communal mercy.
Each soul earns only against itself, no bearer carries another's burden, and all return to their Lord to be informed; earning, individuality, and return converge.
Fear, hunger, and loss are named as tests, giving the living setting in which the patient response of return in 2:156 is formed.
Those patient responders receive blessings, mercy, and guidance from their Lord, completing the favorable consequence of consciously belonging and returning.
Wealth and children are a trial while immense reward is with God, correcting the use of worldly abundance as a measure of final honor.
God's promise is true, so worldly life must not deceive; the warning asks the hearer to relocate confidence before the promised meeting.
The condemned person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, embodying investment in what cannot become lasting provision.
He thinks his wealth has made him immortal, attaching life to possession in the precise way judgment will overturn.
